articles.title: AI solves 79-year-old math mystery of six-dimensional spheres
articles.summary: It asks whether a six-dimensional sphere can be completely described using complex numbers, which include the (seemingly impossible) square root of –1.  This...
articles.body:
He's done it again: mathematician Levent Alpöge, at Anthropic, has solved yet another open math problem using artificial intelligence. He had already tackled the Jacobian conjecture and found two new elliptic curves . Now add to these the 1947 Hopf problem. It asks whether a six-dimensional sphere can be completely described using complex numbers, which include the (seemingly impossible) square root of –1. According to Alpöge, the answer is yes, though the result remains unverified.

Some geometric objects, such as a regular sphere (a two-dimensional surface that lives in three-dimensional space), have a "complex structure." This means that there's a simple way to assign a different complex number to every point on the sphere. The advantage of this is that many more mathematical tools are available for complex numbers than the usual "real" numbers, which makes some calculations easier. The complex structure on the sphere has had far-reaching uses, such as connecting complicated, ugly equations that live on its surface to simple, polynomial equations.

In a 1947 paper, German mathematician Heinz Hopf posed the question: What about higher-dimensional spheres? He showed that, no, high-dimensional spheres don't have a complex structure. But he couldn't prove it for one case: the 6D sphere.

Ever since, numerous experts have grappled with this scenario. They've proposed evidence both for and against the hypothesis that a complex structure exists for the 6D surface of a sphere. But no one has managed to prove their case.

Now AI may have solved the problem. Alpöge used an internal version of Anthropic's large language model, Claude, to do what humans could not. On August 23 Alpöge posted a 100-plus-page document with a purported proof that the 6D sphere does, in fact, have a complex structure. For the proof, the AI apparently generated a complex 3D structure and demonstrated that it exactly represents the 6D surface of a sphere.

Unfortunately, the full document was nigh-indecipherable—LLMs tend to explain their proofs in unhelpful ways, spending inordinate time on minor details while glancing past important steps.

Mathematician Ilka Agricola at the University of Marburg in Germany says this lack of transparency is typical of tech company announcements: "You don't know how many prompts were needed to arrive at the result, how much human fine-tuning was required, and so on." Then, he adds, the mathematical community must verify the claim.

And they got right to work. Within a few days, they'd reconstructed the proof. "There seems to be an emerging consensus that the construction is plausible," says Duke University mathematician Robert L. Bryant. On August 27 Philip Engel of the University of Illinois Chicago posted a more pedagogical explanation of the LLM's process on his website. Around the same time, OpenAI researcher Boris Alexeev managed to formalize the proof, verifying its correctness step-by-step using the programming language Lean.

"These examples of 'new geometry' have become very rare and precious," Engel says. "There is a new geometric object in the world that we now know about and can explore."

Meanwhile, Alpöge has continued to explore other mathematical mysteries. In separate work with mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, he made significant progress toward the Navier-Stokes problem, which made headlines recently when OpenAI claimed to have found a solution.

An earlier version of this article originally appeared in Spektrum der Wissenschaft and was updated with permission. It was translated from the original German version with the assistance of artificial intelligence and reviewed by our editors .

articles.title: After wildfires turned the ground black, grasshoppers rapidly evolved darker colouration; as vegetation returned, black morphs declined
articles.summary: A wildfire can transform a landscape in a matter of hours, leaving behind a ground surface dominated by blackened soil, ash and charred vegetation.
articles.body: A wildfire can transform a landscape in a matter of hours, leaving behind a ground surface dominated by blackened soil, ash and charred vegetation. For the pygmy grasshopper Tetrix subulata, that sudden change appears to have been followed by an equally striking shift in colour. Populations living in recently burned areas of Sweden contained far more black, or melanistic, grasshoppers than those living in nearby unburned habitats. In a study published in Evolution titled Rapid evolution of fire melanism in replicated populations of pygmy grasshoppers, Anders Forsman, Magnus Karlsson, Lena Wennersten, Jenny Johansson and Einat Karpestam compared 20 populations and found that melanistic individuals made up about 50% of the grasshoppers in recently burned areas, compared with roughly 9% in unburned populations. The researchers also found that the frequency of the dark morph fell to about 30% four years after the fire, as the habitat began to recover. Their experiments provided evidence that the differences had a genetic component, suggesting that the changing proportions of dark and light grasshoppers reflected evolutionary change across generations rather than individual insects simply changing colour in response to the blackened ground.The dark morph's advantage faded within just a few yearsThe decline in melanistic grasshoppers as burned habitats recovered was also consistent with earlier research on the species. In a study published in Oecologia titled Dynamics of colour polymorphism in a changing environment: fire melanism and then what?, Magnus Karlsson, Sofia Caesar, Jonas Ahnesjö and Anders Forsman examined colour-pattern dynamics in a natural population of T. subulata inhabiting a previously burned clear-cut area. The researchers found that black phenotypes initially dominated after the fire, but their frequency subsequently declined as the environment changed. The study also documented increasing diversity among colour morphs during the recovery of the habitat. These findings are consistent with the idea that the selective conditions affecting colour can change as a burned landscape develops. Rather than individual grasshoppers becoming black immediately after a fire and then becoming lighter as vegetation returns, the evidence points to changes in the relative frequency of inherited colour variants within the population.Predation by sight-hunting animals appears to drive the patternCamouflage against visually oriented predators has been proposed as one mechanism behind these changes. In a study published in Ecology and Evolution titled Reduced predation risk for melanistic pygmy grasshoppers in post-fire environments, Einat Karpestam, Sami Merilaita and Anders Forsman tested whether the protective value of black colouration changed depending on the visual background. The researchers presented human participants with images of black grasshoppers against samples of natural habitats and measured how easily the insects could be detected. They found that black colouration provided greater protection against detection in backgrounds containing more blackened material from fire. The researchers concluded that the results supported camouflage and predation as important drivers of fire melanism in pygmy grasshoppers. However, the experiment used human observers as model visual predators, so it provides experimental evidence for the camouflage mechanism rather than direct evidence that natural predators alone produced the population-level changes.The findings show how quickly evolutionary change can occurThe grasshopper research is notable because the changes in colour-morph frequency occurred over a relatively short period. The 2011 Evolution study compared populations exposed to different fire histories and found that the frequency of melanistic individuals changed between successive years. Its common-garden breeding experiments were designed to determine whether differences in colour frequencies reflected genetic differences or developmental plasticity. The researchers found evidence that the variation had a genetic basis, meaning that the changing frequencies could represent evolutionary responses to changing selection rather than a temporary colour change experienced by individual insects. The authors described the findings as evidence for extraordinarily rapid contemporary adaptive evolution in replicated natural populations. The important distinction is that the grasshoppers did not individually switch their colour in response to the blackened ground. Instead, the proportion of individuals carrying different inherited colour patterns changed as the environmental conditions changed.The species didn't just turn black and stay that wayThe research therefore points to a more dynamic process than a simple shift toward black colouration after a fire. The 2008 Oecologia study found that after black phenotypes initially became dominant, the distribution of colour morphs changed as the habitat recovered, with greater diversity among the observed patterns. The 2011 Evolution study similarly found that the frequency of melanistic individuals in burned populations declined over four years. Together, the findings suggest that fire can rapidly alter the selective environment experienced by T. subulata, favouring different colour variants at different stages of habitat recovery. Black colouration may provide better camouflage when the ground contains extensive areas of charred material, while that advantage can diminish as vegetation returns and the visual background changes. The result is not a permanent population of black grasshoppers, but a shifting balance among inherited colour forms as the environment itself changes.

articles.title: NASA astronaut John Young carried a corned beef sandwich hidden in his spacesuit aboard Gemini III in 1965; rye crumbs floated through the cabin, and it became a $30 million problem for NASA
articles.summary: NASA astronaut John W.
articles.body: NASA astronaut John W. Young secretly carried a freshly made corned-beef sandwich on rye into space during the Gemini III mission on March 23, 1965, hiding it in a pocket of his spacesuit. Nearly two hours into the flight, Young pulled it out and offered some to commander Virgil 'Gus' Grissom. The rye bread quickly crumbled, sending pieces floating inside the cabin and raising concerns about debris getting into equipment or an astronaut's eyes. What began as a practical joke soon became a serious issue back on Earth. The episode reached a US House appropriations hearing, where the sandwich was mocked in the press as the '$30 million sandwich', a reference to the estimated $30 million cost of the Gemini III mission. NASA subsequently tightened rules on what astronauts could take aboard spacecraft.Why NASA astronaut John Young brought a sandwich into spaceGemini III was the first crewed mission of NASA's Gemini programme and the first US spaceflight to carry two astronauts. Young served as pilot, while Grissom was the command pilot. The mission launched on March 23, 1965, and lasted about 4 hours and 52 minutes, completing three orbits of Earth. One of the mission's secondary objectives was to evaluate NASA's newly developed space-food system. The astronauts had practised eating specially prepared meals that were freeze-dried or otherwise packaged so they could be rehydrated and consumed in microgravity. The food was functional, but it was not particularly popular with the astronauts. Young later explained that Grissom had become bored with the food they had been eating during training. The idea of bringing a conventional sandwich into space therefore seemed amusing. Fellow astronaut Walter 'Wally' Schirra, who was the backup command pilot for Gemini III, bought a corned-beef sandwich from a restaurant in Cocoa Beach, Florida. Young then slipped it into a pocket of his pressure suit before launch.The sandwich appeared nearly two hours into the flightThe sandwich remained hidden until Young began the mission's food and waste evaluation roughly two hours after launch. He pulled it from his spacesuit and offered it to Grissom. According to NASA's account of the flight, Grissom asked Young what it was and where it came from. Young acknowledged that he had brought it with him and suggested that they see how it tasted. Grissom took a bite, but the sandwich immediately demonstrated why conventional bread was unsuitable for a spacecraft. The rye bread began breaking apart, with crumbs floating around the cabin. Grissom put the unfinished sandwich into his own spacesuit pocket in an attempt to keep the crumbs contained. NASA says the exchange lasted less than a minute. There was also the smell. Contemporary accounts describe the strong aroma of corned beef filling the small spacecraft. NASA's historical record notes that Grissom was surprised by the sandwich and its pungent smell.Why a few crumbs became a serious problemThe incident may sound trivial today, but loose food particles could create genuine problems inside a spacecraft. The Gemini cabin contained instruments, switches and other equipment that had to function reliably. Floating crumbs could potentially become lodged behind instrument panels or interfere with equipment. They could also get into an astronaut's eyes. NASA's historical account specifically notes these concerns. The approved Gemini food system had been designed partly to avoid this problem. Food was packaged in ways that reduced loose particles, while some items were coated or compressed to make them easier to handle in microgravity. The sandwich therefore provided an accidental demonstration of why NASA had been so careful about space-food design. Importantly, NASA says the sandwich did not damage the spacecraft or disrupt the mission's experiments. The agency's later historical account states that there was no detriment to the experimental programme or the actual conduct of Gemini III because of the sandwich.The '$30 million sandwich' reached CongressThe story became much bigger after Gemini III returned to Earth. At a post-flight press conference in Cocoa Beach, reporters asked Young about the sandwich, and the incident soon attracted the attention of lawmakers during hearings on NASA's 1966 budget. Representative George E. Shipley of Illinois criticised the decision to bring an unauthorised sandwich aboard the spacecraft, comparing the tightly controlled cabin to a surgeon's operating room. NASA Associate Administrator George Mueller told the House Committee on Appropriations that the agency had taken steps to prevent another corned-beef sandwich from being carried on a future mission.The famous '$30 million sandwich' nickname came from the estimated cost of the Gemini III mission, not from the value of the food. Young later recalled that some members of Congress believed the astronauts had brought the sandwich into a mission that was specifically supposed to evaluate approved space food, raising concerns that the stunt could undermine an extremely expensive government-funded programme. One committee member therefore used the '$30 million' figure to highlight the disproportion between the cheap sandwich and the enormous cost of the mission. NASA's official history cites the Evening Star headline “$30 Million Sandwich”: House Doesn't Relish Astronauts' Snack, published on April 15, 1965.NASA subsequently tightened its rules. Beginning with Gemini IV, astronauts were required to provide lists of items they intended to take aboard, and sandwiches were specifically prohibited.NASA banned sandwiches, but Young's career continuedThe sandwich episode had a practical consequence. Beginning with Gemini IV, NASA required crews to provide a list of items they intended to take aboard their spacecraft. Sandwiches were specifically prohibited, along with certain bulky, heavy or metallic objects that could interfere with spacecraft equipment. Astronauts could still carry approved personal items in their personal preference kits.Young did not receive a formal reprimand, although NASA made clear that officials and lawmakers were unhappy with the stunt. Other astronauts were advised not to repeat similar pranks. The incident ultimately became a tiny footnote in Young's extraordinary career. He went on to fly six space missions, including two Gemini flights, two Apollo missions and two Space Shuttle missions. He commanded STS-1, the first Space Shuttle mission, and served as chief of NASA's Astronaut Office for 13 years.The irony continued decades later. NASA eventually became more accommodating of sandwiches and bread-based foods in space. During Apollo 13, astronauts had bread and sandwich fillings available, although NASA had developed much better food systems by then.The Gemini III sandwich itself became part of spaceflight folklore. A replica preserved in resin has been displayed at the Grissom Memorial Museum in Mitchell, Indiana, commemorating the snack that briefly became one of NASA's strangest controversies.

articles.title: Indonesia's rainforest regenerated for a decade; 43.8% of bird species increased, but trapping pressure was linked to slower recovery
articles.summary: A decade of forest regeneration in Indonesia’s Harapan Rainforest was linked to rising bird abundance, with 43.8% of bird species showing significant
articles.body: A decade of forest regeneration in Indonesia’s Harapan Rainforest was linked to rising bird abundance, with 43.8% of bird species showing significant increases, according to a study published in Biological Conservation. Researchers surveyed birds between 2009–2011 and again in 2018, recording 187 species across the two periods. However, the study found evidence that trapping pressure increasingly affected bird populations as the forest became more accessible. According to the study published in ScienceDirect, titled ‘Avifauna recovers faster in areas less accessible to trapping in regenerating tropical forests’, the proportion of species with significantly higher abundance in less accessible areas rose from 5.4% to 16.2%. Researchers also found that 14% of species did not recover as quickly as predicted from forest regeneration alone, highlighting the impact associated with wildlife trapping.How did 43.8% of bird species respond to rainforest recoveryThe researchers recorded 187 bird species across the two survey periods. Of these, 122 species were recorded during both periods and were included in the abundance modelling. Among those 122 species, 45.1% showed significantly greater mean abundance in the current period than in the early period, while no species showed a statistically significant decline in mean abundance over time. The researchers reported an average community-level increase in abundance, although the estimated interval meant that this overall change was not statistically significant.The study's headline figure of 43.8% refers to the broader result reported in the abstract: forest regeneration was associated with significant abundance increases for 43.8% of bird species over the decade. The researchers nevertheless found that forest recovery did not occur in isolation from other pressures. Their results showed that forests had also become more accessible to people during the study period, with mean access difficulty falling from 1.32 kilometres during the early period to 0.72 kilometres in 2018. The researchers used accessibility as a proxy for trapping pressure because direct measurement of trapping activity across the landscape was difficult.How did trapping pressure affect bird abundanceThe proportion of species whose abundance significantly increased as access difficulty increased rose from 5.4% in the early period to 16.2% in the current period. The researchers interpreted higher abundance in less accessible areas as being likely linked to the negative effects of trapping, because more remote locations were harder for people to reach. They also found that 48.4% of species increased in the degree to which their abundance was associated with increasing access difficulty.The study also found evidence of a recovery deficit associated with intensified trapping. Fifteen per cent of the species analysed exhibited a significant recovery deficit, meaning their observed abundance was lower than the researchers' counterfactual estimate under a scenario in which trapping pressure had not intensified. The deficit was concentrated in areas with greater human accessibility, with the researchers identifying a zone of reduced recovery around easier-access locations. In the abstract, the authors similarly reported that 14% of species did not recover as fast as predicted based on observed forest regeneration over the study period.Bird trapping differs between targeted and opportunistic speciesTargeted species included birds prized for singing abilities, ornamental attractiveness or body parts, while opportunistically trapped species were those not specifically targeted but still captured and sold when possible. A higher proportion of targeted species showed a significant positive relationship between abundance and access difficulty in 2018, while targeted species also had a higher proportion showing a significant recovery deficit.The researchers also found that forest-dependent species were more strongly associated with less accessible areas than generalist species in the current period and had greater recovery deficits. Their conclusion states that “species prized in the pet trade and those dependent on late-successional forest habitat were particularly concentrated in remote, inaccessible areas”. The study therefore describes two simultaneous patterns at Harapan: bird abundance increased during forest regeneration, while trapping pressure was associated with slower recovery for some species and greater abundance in areas farther from human access.

articles.title: Tanzania planted 100,000 native trees along an elephant corridor; the 1,000 animals now have a route from savanna to rainforest
articles.summary: Tanzania has officially protected a narrow wildlife corridor linking Nyerere National Park’s savanna woodlands with the rainforests of the Udzungwa
articles.body: Tanzania has officially protected a narrow wildlife corridor linking Nyerere National Park’s savanna woodlands with the rainforests of the Udzungwa Mountains. The Nyerere-Udzungwa Wildlife Corridor crosses the Kilombero Valley, where farm fields had divided the elephants’ old natural path, making it harder for them to move between the savanna and rainforest. Around 1,000 elephants use this landscape, moving between lowland and mountain habitats. Since restoration began, local communities and conservation groups have planted 100,000 native trees and introduced measures to guide elephants away from farms. The corridor was formally recognised by Tanzania in April 2025, giving legal protection to the route.How 100,000 native trees helped restore the landscape for the elephantsRestoring vegetation became an important part of making the corridor useful to wildlife. Southern Tanzania Elephant Program(STEP) reports that its partner Reforest Africa has planted 100,000 tree seedlings using indigenous species, alongside assisted natural regeneration.The World Land Trust says its 2025 Plant a Tree project is supporting restoration in the Greater Udzungwa-Kilombero landscape. The programme provided funding for 100,000 native trees to restore 100 hectares of degraded land in the Magombera Nature Forest Reserve. It also supports a nursery and training hub intended to help plant another 50,000 native trees across a further 50 hectares.Mongabay reported that the first 100,000 trees planted inside the corridor represent about 30 species. Some areas are being planted densely to recreate forest, while other sections are being kept more open to provide woodland habitat. Species have also been selected for the food they provide to different animals. Fruits from sycamore figs and wild mangoes, for example, are eaten by Sykes’ monkeys and trumpeter hornbills.The trees are already changing the appearance of parts of the valley. According to Mongabay, trees planted in late 2023 had grown above head height, with their expanding green cover visible in satellite images.The elephant corridor connects savanna to rainforestThe corridor stretches for about 14 kilometres across the Kilombero Valley, linking Nyerere National Park and the Magombera Nature Forest Reserve in the east with Udzungwa Mountains National Park in the west. Mongabay reported that the route is only about 200 metres wide in places, making the protected strip a narrow passage through a heavily used agricultural landscape.STEP reports that the corridor reconnects habitats that had been separated after forests were cleared and land was converted to farms. The organisation began working with villages and the Tanzanian government in 2018 to restore the route. On 4 April 2025, the government officially designated it as Tanzania’s first wildlife corridor with this legal status.The route matters because elephants do not remain in one type of habitat throughout the year. Mongabay reported that elephants in this region move between mountain and lowland forests, miombo woodland and open bush. During dry periods, the mountains can provide food and water when lower areas become less suitable.Why was the route needed after forests disappearedThe landscape was not always divided in the way it is today. According to Mongabay, about 50 years ago the valley was connected by lowland rainforest. Much of that forest was later cleared as agriculture expanded, leaving elephants to cross farmland along routes they had used for generations.That movement created problems for both wildlife and farmers. STEP reports that 3 villages involved in the corridor agreed to set aside about 7% of their village land. A total of 368 landowners were compensated for their farm plots, with roughly 2.2 billion Tanzanian shillings raised for direct compensation to households.Measures to keep elephants away from farmsTrees alone cannot make the route safe. The project has also used fencing to guide elephants towards the corridor and reduce encounters with people. Fondazione Capellino reports the initiative as a 13-kilometre ecological corridor and says Tanzania’s first large-scale electric fencing system is being used to reduce human-elephant conflict.The foundation reports that elephants have increasingly remained within the corridor during daylight, gathering in shaded areas and near streams. It also says that residents in Upogoroni sub-village, who previously had to leave their fields in the afternoon because of elephant movements, can now work in their fields during the day.The fencing system is still being improved. Fondazione Capellino says severe flooding in early 2026 led to another technical planning phase, while a redesigned system is intended to cope better with seasonal floods. By early 2026, fencing had reached about 12.6 kilometres, with further work planned.What has the corridor revealed about wildlife useMonitoring has shown that the route is already being used by a range of animals. STEP says biodiversity monitoring recorded 26 species of large and medium-sized mammals in the corridor and detected increased elephant use.Mongabay reported that 59 camera traps installed across the corridor recorded at least 1,440 mammals during a 15-month period, including 529 elephants. The cameras also recorded species such as buffalo, bushbuck, serval, honey badgers, Sykes’ monkeys and Cape clawless otters. The corridor is serving a wider purpose than simply moving elephants between two protected areas.Challenges for the restored corridorThe official designation has strengthened protection, but the project still faces practical challenges. Mongabay reported that elephants have not yet consistently used an underpass beneath a busy road near the Udzungwa Mountains. Crowds gathering to watch the animals can cause them to turn back, while planned development close to the corridor could create additional pressure.Fondazione Capellino reports that fencing, monitoring, patrols and community involvement remain ongoing rather than completed tasks.

articles.title: A Norfolk seal was rescued with 4 kilograms of fishing debris wrapped around her neck; the material had cut a 3-inch-deep wound and she now faces months of rehabilitation if she survives
articles.summary: A young gray seal caught in a snare of discarded fishing gear that had tightened around her neck has a long road to recovery.
articles.body: A young gray seal caught in a snare of discarded fishing gear that had tightened around her neck has a long road to recovery. By the time rescuers reached her, the debris had cut through her and left her nearly unable to move through the water, states an online report by Broadland Radio. Her caregivers named the seal Donut and she was found at Horsey on September 20 in a condition that left little room for delay. She is now being cared for by specialists at the RSPCA’s East Winch Wildlife Center and her survival remains uncertain, adds the online report.Four kilos of wreckageDonut, about a year old, had become ensnared in a tangle of netting, twine, fishing hooks and metal. The material was tight against her neck now, a heavy collar that still hurt when she moved. When rescuers finally freed her the tangled mess weighed around four kilos. The debris had cut deep into the seal’s neck, causing a wound some three inches deep. The injury was painful, and it also threatened her ability to swim and hunt, skills that a young seal needs to survive in the wild. With help from members of the public, volunteers from Friends of Horsey Seals managed to get Donut onto a stretcher and safely remove her from the beach.The road ahead is hardDonut was taken to the RSPCA East Winch Wildlife Center for emergency veterinary treatment. She is still in critical condition and the priority now is to treat her serious wound and stabilize her health. She is expected to pull through the initial ordeal but her recovery will be a long one. It will be several months before she is strong enough to go back to sea, and that will be with treatment and rehab, states the online report. For a young seal already weakened by injury the process will involve rebuilding her strength and ensuring she can once again swim, feed and fend for herself in the wild.The shore line is a red flagDoughnut’s plight reflects a continuing danger to marine wildlife around the British coast. Fishing line, netting, hooks, ropes and other discarded materials can persist in the marine environment long after they have fulfilled their original function. Animals can become entangled while swimming, feeding or resting, and injuries can be exacerbated as the material constricts around their bodies. Doughnut’s case was a few kilograms of debris that became a potentially deadly trap.Her rescue also emphasizes the necessity of promptly reporting animals in distress and involving trained wildlife rescuers. The next few months will tell if Donut can recover from her injuries and make it back to the Norfolk coast. The young seal is currently in specialist care, and her survival depends on treatment, rehabilitation and time, concludes the report.Image Courtesy: istock

articles.title: California crews digging 12 feet below an Oceanside infrastructure project uncovered limb bones, ribs and fragments that paleontologists say may belong to a ‘thunder beast’ up to 45 million years old
articles.summary: A routine infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, has led to an unexpected discovery from deep beneath the ground: fossilised bones that may have
articles.body: A routine infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, has led to an unexpected discovery from deep beneath the ground: fossilised bones that may have belonged to a huge hoofed mammal that lived as long as 45 million years ago. According to the City of Oceanside, which announced the discovery, crews uncovered several limb bones, ribs and other fragments about 12 feet below the surface. Paleontologists believe the remains could belong to a prehistoric animal known as a “thunder beast”; another possibility is a creature known as a “swamp rhino”. Researchers are now studying the fossils to determine the animal's exact identity.Fossils emerge during routine constructionThe discovery was made recently while crews were carrying out excavation for a city infrastructure project in Oceanside, about 40 miles north of San Diego. Workers digging roughly 12 feet below the surface came across several fossilised bones embedded in hardened sedimentary rock. The remains included multiple limb bones, ribs and numerous other bones and fragments. Their size and shape suggested to paleontologists that they belonged to a large hoofed mammal that lived in the region during the Eocene Epoch.The fossils were found in what the City of Oceanside describes as “Member C of the Santiago Formation,” a thick sequence of sedimentary rock in northwestern San Diego County. The formation dates to a period when the landscape of present-day Southern California was very different from what it is today. Rather than stopping construction entirely, the discovery prompted paleontologists to secure the area and carefully excavate the remains.Seven days of careful excavationJoseph El Adli, a paleontologist who was monitoring the construction site, recognised the importance of the discovery and led additional excavation work. According to the City of Oceanside, El Adli's team spent seven days exposing the fossils from beneath several tons of hardened mudstone and sandstone. The bones were then placed inside a protective plaster field jacket so they could be transported safely to an off-site laboratory for further preparation.The fossils are still encased in rock, meaning researchers have not yet been able to examine every part of the specimens. That is also why the precise identity of the animal remains uncertain. The exact location of the discovery is not disclosed yet, citing public safety concerns and the need to protect the site.Was it a ‘thunder beast’ or a swamp rhino?Based on the size and shape of the recovered bones, El Adli believes the animal could belong to one of two groups of extinct mammals. One possibility is a Titanothere, commonly referred to as a “thunder beast”. These were large, hoofed mammals that lived in North America during the Eocene. They were members of the extinct brontothere group and could reach considerable sizes.The second possibility is an Amynodon, sometimes described as a “swamp rhino”. Despite the name, these animals were not modern rhinoceroses. They belonged to an extinct group of large-bodied mammals and are thought to have had adaptations associated with life around wetlands. At this stage, paleontologists have not confirmed which of the two animals the Oceanside fossils represent. Further preparation and examination of the bones should help narrow down their identity.A glimpse into ancient OceansideThe fossils provide a window into a period when the landscape around present-day Oceanside was home to very different animals and environments. Officials said the mammal lived on ancient floodplains roughly 40 million to 45 million years ago. The rocks surrounding the remains belong to the Eocene-aged Santiago Formation and fall within the Uintan North American Land Mammal Age. The find also adds to evidence that the region contains significant fossil deposits. According to the Los Angeles Times, other fossils have previously been recovered from the Santiago Formation, including remains of early saber-toothed carnivores and primates.Modern construction has also uncovered fossils elsewhere in Southern California, demonstrating how buried geological deposits can sometimes remain hidden until excavation reaches them.What happens to the fossils next?The recovered specimens are expected to undergo further preparation and scientific examination once researchers remove more of the surrounding rock. The additional work could reveal features that distinguish a thunder beast from a swamp rhino and provide more information about the animal's size and biology. The researchers will also be able to determine whether the fragments belong to a single individual. The City of Oceanside said the specimens are ultimately expected to become part of a museum collection, where they can be preserved and made available to scientists and the public for further study.For now, the discovery remains a scientific mystery. What began as a routine excavation 12 feet beneath an Oceanside construction project has instead uncovered bones from an animal that may have walked across Southern California's ancient floodplains tens of millions of years ago. Further examination of the fossils will determine whether the long-buried remains belonged to a “thunder beast”, a swamp rhino or another prehistoric mammal.

articles.title: In 1984, NASA sent 12.5 million tomato seeds to space; in 1990 they had to be brought back to Earth and were planted across 40,000 schools in 40 countries
articles.summary: The seeds that NASA sent to space in 1984, returned to Earth six years later in 1990 and had to be distributed among students as plant kits.
articles.body: The seeds that NASA sent to space in 1984, returned to Earth six years later in 1990 and had to be distributed among students as plant kits. What lies behind this statement is a tale of space motion that many remain unaware of. The mission was to determine whether exposure to the space environment would affect the germination and plant growth of the seeds, but the agency was never able to observe the same.A hopeful experimentThe project was called SEEDS, which stands for Space Exposed Experiment Developed for Students. It involved NASA headquarters, the Langley Research Centre and the company George W. Park Seed, a traditional seed supplier in US. The idea was to send a group of seeds into space and keep a group on Earth. Then, both sets of identical seeds would be distributed to the schools so that students could plant them side by side and compare the results.All 12.5 million seeds belonged to the variety Rutgers California Supreme, a common tomato in American cultivation. This was chosen because using a single variety prevents genetic differences from skewing the results. The equipment that carried the seeds into space was the Long Duration Exposure Facility (LDEF), a twelve-sided cylindrical structure, weighing about 9.7 tons, designed to remain stationary in space while experiments attached to its surface were exposed to vacuum, radiation and micrometeorites. The LDEF had no propulsion or power generation of its own. It was built to be released by one space shuttle and collected by another, and it carried dozens of experiments from various countries, not just the seed experiments.The Space Shuttle Challenger released the LDEF into orbit on April 7, 1984, during the STC-41 C mission. The plan was to retrieve it within a year during a subsequent, pre-scheduled mission. Two years later, the same shuttle exploded 73 seconds after launch on January 28, 1986, killing all seven crew members. The entire fleet was grounded, and planned missions were reorganised.Without an engine to correct its trajectory, the LDEF gradually lost altitude, slowed by the residual atmosphere that exists even hundreds of kilometres up. Over the years, its orbit dropped to about 280 kilometres. When the rescue finally arrived, the platform was mere weeks away from re-entering the atmosphere and disintegrating. In this case, the 12.5 million seeds would have burned up as well.The Space Shuttle Columbia captured the platform on January 12, 1990, during the STS-32 mission, bringing it back with the seeds intact. Combined, this amounted to 69 months in orbit, nearly six years and over 32,000 orbits around Earth. The seeds remained sealed in containers inside the platform, with no cultivation in orbit. Nothing germinated in space; the exposure was only to the environment. During this time, they were exposed to solar radiation, cosmic rays and microgravity.Planting kits for studentsAfter the return, as planned, the educational phase of the project began. According to a NASA educational report, approximately 132,000 planting kits were distributed to teachers at about 40,000 schools, reaching about 3.3 million students. The outreach covered all 50 US states, the District of Columbia and another 30 countries across the world. It included classes from preschool to universities.Each kit contained both group of seeds, the ones that had spent nearly six years in space and the ones that had been stored in a controlled environment for the same duration. This second group is what science refers to as the control: it serves as a benchmark to determine whether any observed differences were actually due to the journey, rather than the variety or planting method. The kits included forms to record any observations made.Students recorded how many seeds germinated, how long it took for the first sprout to appear and how the plants developed over the weeks. They also noted the appearance of the flowers, formation of the fruit and the condition of leaves and stems. The recorded data was sent back to NASA which compiled the information for analysis. The agency received nearly 8,000 reports submitted by entire classes.Preliminary data showed a germination rate of 73.8% for the space seeds, compared to 70.3% for the Earth seeds. In tests conducted in the first six months after retrieval, the space seeds averaged germination in 8 days, while the Earth seeds took 8.3 days. There was also a tendency for initial growth to be faster in the first three to four weeks. After this period, the terrestrial plants caught up to the others.The project’s summary did not identify any overall differences between the two groups of plants or their fruits. The small initial advantages did not persist through the end of the cycle.SEEDS (Space Exposed Experiment Developed for Students) has become one of the largest science projects ever conducted in classrooms with material that has been exposed to space, both in terms of participant numbers and geographical reach.

articles.title: Famed spy plane disappears from California air base as mystery grows
articles.summary: A Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird strategic reconnaissance aircraft is pictured. The SR-71 is the fastest, highest flying air-breathing aircraft in the world, flyin...
articles.body:
A Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird spy plane has disappeared from a California military base, sparking speculation about its potential connection to NASA's mysterious new aircraft.

The missing SR-71 Blackbird, tail No. 844, was the last of its kind to fly, making its final flight in 1999, and had been displayed at NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center for years before its disappearance.

NASA is rebuilding its fleet of experimental X-planes and focusing on extreme-speed and high-altitude flight research, with the missing jet's whereabouts currently unknown but speculation about a potential return-to-flight program after more than 26 years.

A legendary spy plane has vanished from a California military base — it comes as NASA teases a mysterious new aircraft sparking speculation the two could be related.

The SR-71 Blackbird, tail No. 844, had been displayed for years at NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center, which is collocated with Edwards Air Force Base.

Satellite imagery indicates it has not been seen since at least May 17, according to Aviation Week defense editor Steve Trimble, who first reported the disappearance.

The timing is hard to ignore. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman unveiled a silhouette resembling an SR-71 during last week's All-In Summit in Los Angeles while promising that the agency is rebuilding its fleet of experimental X-planes and pushing back into extreme-speed and high-altitude flight research.

"In the service of the first A [aeronautics] in NASA, we are rebuilding our X-plane fleet. The X-59 is researching quiet supersonic flight, but it's just the beginning," Isaacman told TWZ .

"It will not be long before NASA once again is flying as high and as fast as we had in decades past, and then even more."

When the Blackbird-like image came up during a live interview immediately afterward, Isaacman added fuel to the mystery by asking, "You sure that's a Blackbird?" He offered no further clarification.

The missing jet is no ordinary exhibit. Originally designated US Air Force serial No. 61-7980, it was the last SR-71 produced and the last one to fly, making its final flight in 1999.

Its current whereabouts are unclear, although Aviation Week sources said the aircraft was moved into a hangar earlier this year for an inspection.

The report said the combination of the jet's disappearance and Isaacman's presentation raises the possibility of a return-to-flight program after more than 26 years.

NASA has not confirmed that scenario, instead pointing to Isaacman's broader push for more experimental aircraft capable of advancing high-speed and high-altitude flight.

The California desert has long been a proving ground for aviation's wildest experiments, and NASA is once again pushing the limits there. The agency's experimental X-59 has been ripping across the skies above the Mojave as part of its effort to make supersonic flight over land quieter.

The sleek aircraft has already reached more than Mach 1 during testing at Edwards, with NASA planning further flights to study the "quiet thump" it produces instead of the ear-splitting sonic boom associated with traditional supersonic jets.

The ultimate goal is to gather enough data to help clear the way for commercial aircraft that could someday slash cross-country flight times.

articles.title: The Aeropod automates soil aeration without robotics — see it at TechCrunch Disrupt | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Muju Earth Technologies has developed a deceptively simply pod that can save farmers money while improving crop yields.
articles.body:
Farmers around the world face a pressing problem: The equipment they use to till, plant, and harvest their fields is killing their margins. Studies have estimated that soil compaction can reduce yields by 20% to 60% .

Plowing can help, but it’s a laborious and expensive task that harms soil health in different ways. Muju Earth has developed an alternative, the Aeropod, that automatically aerates the soil without machinery or robotics. The startup says it can promote better soil health while cutting farmers’ tilling costs by half or more.

The device is “built like a seed, it sows like a seed, and it ships like a seed,” Ifeoluwa Afolayan, the company’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. The device is about the size of a fingernail, and farmers drop it in the soil alongside their seeds using the same equipment. There’s no need to till the soil in advance.

“It just really seems like a no-brainer,” Afolayan said.

After the Aeropod is exposed to a combination of temperature, pressure, and moisture, it bursts open, loosening the soil and creating small channels that let air, water, and roots move through it more easily.

Muju Earth — one of the 200 startups in this year’s Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco in October — has tested its devices in lab settings and is embarking on paid field trials this fall in the U.K. Nine farmers are participating, and the startup has more than 30 on a waitlist.

Its initial target market is onion growers in the U.K. since onions are particularly sensitive to soil compaction, Afolayan said.

Tilling a field once might cost around £250 to £400 per hectare when factoring in labor costs, diesel, and wear and tear on equipment, Afolayan said. The Aeropod should produce similar results at just £100 per hectare, Afolayan said.

The Aeropod was born during Afolayan’s and co-founder Wangyang Hu’s time at Imperial College London, where they sought to design a product that would improve farmers’ bottom lines while also aiding soil health. The Aeropod’s development was driven by a single question: “How do you make this as simple as sowing a seed?” Afolayan said. “That’s the most equitable practice across every farmer on the planet.”

In addition to farmers, the startup has also heard from companies developing biologic amendments — products added to soil, often containing living microbes, that boost or replace chemical fertilizers. Because those companies’ products work best in aerated soils, they’re interested in pairing with the Aeropod.

But Afolayan said that farmers have been leading adoption. Most of the marketing to date has been inbound. “The best thing about Aeropod is the farmers intuitively understand the proposition,” she said.

Muju Earth is one of 200 startups in this year’s Startup Battlefield , a pitch competition in which 20 finalists will present on the main stage at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place October 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco.

articles.title: Fury v Joshua Cardiff fight set to provide big boost to the economy
articles.summary: Cardiff is preparing for an influx of fans from across the globe for the 11 December showdown.
articles.body:
Business owners expect the much anticipated clash between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury to provide a "big boost" to the Welsh economy.

The British heavyweights are set to fight on 11 December at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, with fans expected to travel to the Welsh capital from all corners of the globe.

A bar manager intends to order triple his usual amount of beer barrels, but some residents have expressed concern about the impact the fight will have on public services.

Transport for Wales said it intends to put extra services on to deal with the influx of fans, as hotel prices for that weekend sky rocket due to increased demand.

Chairman of Cardiff Night Forum Nick Newman said he was "absolutely delighted" by the announcement, as another "fantastic showpiece" is coming to the city.

He manages nine pubs, and said venue owners across the city will be planning, getting beer in the cellar and food in the fridges.

Newman said he has "no concerns" about the scale of the event, with planning meetings set to take place in the months leading up.

He said they have agreed with Cardiff council and South Wales Police licensing that businesses can apply for an extended hours license.

"That means we can serve alcohol until 05:30, and then close the premises at 06:00," he added.

Newman said this would allow the city to "reset" for any workers in the city centre on Saturday morning.

He expects there to be a similar level of excitement to Joe Calzaghe's fight against Mikkel Kessler in 2007, when more than 50,000 fans descended on what was then the Millennium Stadium.

"That's great for the economy. That's great for jobs. That's great for the sort of feel-good factor around the city," he added.

Twm Jones, assistant manager of On the River, a venue opposite the Principality Stadium, says they are "really excited" for the event.

The bar opened on the first weekend of the Oasis tour, which kicked off in Cardiff , which gave him a sense of how busy the city can be when big events take place.

"We'll probably be buying in triple the amount of barrels that we usually would," he said.

They expect to have a couple of hundred people in the venue on fight night and Jones said they intend to stay open until "at least before the fight, and probably after as well".

"It gets a bit rowdy but its all good fun," he added.

But Sarah Hill, who lives close the Principality Stadium, disagrees and says she "doesn't see the appeal" of the fight.

"Why are they doing it? I don't really pay attention to boxing at all," she added.

Hill realises that Cardiff is no stranger to hosting big events, but said "every big event at the Principality Stadium is an inconvenience to the people that live here".

"Rock concerts, rugby games. Any kind of sporting event is just a nightmare," she added.

"The entire city shuts. So if you want to get from the train station to your house, you have to go out of your way just to get a taxi."

She said the taxis can "cost a fortune" on event days, due to surge pricing, and the late start time has also left her questioning how Cardiff's infrastructure will cope, with the event feeling like "it's just about money".

"The trains only run so late so it's just about selling as much booze before and after the event," Hill added.

"If the start time is there to benefit the audience in the United States, why is it even here?"

Jack Gower moved to Cardiff this month for his university studies and said it has become a "big event city" in recent years.

"It's good because any big event in the UK you think London or Manchester. It's good for cities like Cardiff to get the publicity," he added.

Jack said he is not much of a sports fan, but admits the event is likely to "impact everyone in some way".

He added: "Especially for local bars and tourist places. Uni students moving in will probably be the biggest thing [boost for bars], and this will just boost the economy more for them."

Dave Leyshon runs DTL Travel, an online travel business based in Pontypridd, Rhondda Cynon Taf, and is selling tickets for the heavyweight clash costing between £450 and £12,000.

"I know it's not a title fight but it's two former heavyweight champions. It's a fair price when you compare it to other major sporting events such as the football World Cup," he said.

Leyshon has called on TfW to "get the travel right" after the fight night rail service was criticised when Joshua fought in Cardiff in 2018.

"That's so important and I know some coach firms locally to me and also in west Wales will be running buses in case people fear there'll be an issue with the trains," he added.

It has almost been 20 years since Joe Calzaghe defeated Kessler at the stadium.

Former stadium manager, Gerry Toms, was in charge then, and said it was a "challenge" putting on a fight in the early hours, but staffing was key.

"A lot of the planning is needed with the police, the rail network, the council, hoteliers, and the taxi services," he said.

"It all has to be coordinated to provide the best possible service you can."

A 22:30 curfew was implemented that night to get the fans into the stadium early, ensuring they would not "descend on the stadium" just before the fight began.

"We still had a couple of fights in the stadium, which weren't in the ring, but good stewarding can keep that calm and step in early to defuse it, " he said.

Executive director of UKHospitality Cymru David Chapman said the fight is going to provide a "big boost" to Cardiff's hospitality businesses, with demand for hotels in the city "incredibly high".

He urged fans to be patient with hotel staff who are dealing with an influx of requests and enquiries.

A spokesperson for Transport for Wales said they are working closely with the event organisers to provide "additional capacity into Cardiff" to help customers return home during early hours of the morning.

They added: "We're now working on a provisional service plan and for all the other arrangements needed to host an event of this size in Cardiff.

"We'll release further information in due course."

articles.title: Niger releases 8 North African ostriches into the wild after the species disappeared from the country; the last wild birds vanished in 2004
articles.summary: Niger has released eight North African ostriches into the wild, bringing the species back to an area where it had disappeared decades ago.
articles.body: Niger has released eight North African ostriches into the wild, bringing the species back to an area where it had disappeared decades ago. On 2 September 2026, 5 females and 3 males were released into the Gadabedji Biosphere Reserve, marking the first reintroduction of the species there. The move follows years of captive breeding and preparation involving Nigerien authorities, conservation organisations and local communities. Sahara Conservation said the release begins a new phase in efforts to establish a self-sustaining wild population of the North African ostrich in Niger.Why were North African ostriches released into the wild in NigerThe release is part of a wider effort to restore the North African ostrich to parts of its former range. The species, also known as the red-necked ostrich, once lived across large areas of the Sahara and Sahel. However, its numbers fell sharply because of hunting, egg collection and the loss and degradation of its habitat.Sahara Conservation explains that the species has disappeared from most of its former Sahelo-Saharan range, apart from a few small savanna populations. In Niger, the species became extinct in the wild in 2004. The organisation has been working to produce enough birds through captive breeding so that small groups can eventually be returned safely to natural habitats.The Gadabedji Biosphere Reserve was selected as the starting point for this work because it formed part of the ostrich’s historical range. Sahara Conservation’s September 2026 news release says the reserve had not seen a wild North African ostrich since 1955.How the population was prepared for its returnThe return to the wild was not the result of a single release. It followed years of breeding, animal care and preparation in Niger.According to Sahara Conservation, the organisation began working with the Saint Louis Zoo, the AZA Struthioniformes Taxon Advisory Group and the Nigerien NGO CERNK in 2007. The partnership helped establish a breeding programme at Kellé in central Niger. Since 2011, Sahara Conservation has managed the site, while training and employing Nigerien staff to care for the birds.A second breeding site at Mainé-Soroa in southern Niger received support from Sahara Conservation from 2017. Improvements at the breeding facilities included better infrastructure, diets, enclosures and animal care. These changes helped increase survival and breeding success.The work also involved moving birds and eggs between breeding sites. This helped maintain genetic diversity and reduce the risk of inbreeding, according to the Kolmården Foundation.Preparation before the 8 birds were releasedPreparation for the Gadabedji release had already begun several years earlier. Sahara Conservation states that its first transfer of North African ostriches to a protected area in Niger took place in 2020, when birds were moved to the Gadabedji Biosphere Reserve with the intention of eventually returning the species to the wild.The Kolmården Foundation reports that 11 ostrich chicks were moved to an acclimatisation pen at Gadabedji in 2021 and 2022. The birds were therefore given time in a controlled environment before the wider reintroduction effort moved forward.At the breeding centres, the birds received regular health checks, while staff monitored their behaviour and access to food and water. Kolmården also says both natural and artificial hatching methods were used to increase the number of surviving chicks. Chick vaccination, including protection against Newcastle disease at Kellé, was another part of the programme.How will the released ostriches be monitoredThe 8 birds released in September form what Sahara Conservation describes as the first founder group. Their release is only an early stage of the wider recovery programme.Teams will monitor the ostriches to see how they adapt to the reserve, survive and move through their new surroundings. Over time, monitoring will also look for reproduction. The goal is not simply to increase the number of birds released, but to establish a population that can survive and reproduce without continued dependence on captive breeding.Before the release, Sahara Conservation and the Gadabedji Protected Area Management Unit also worked with local administrative and traditional authorities to explain the project to nearby communities. Almost 260 people from 9 villages attended information meetings covering the ostrich, its role in the ecosystem, the purpose of the reintroduction and ways people and wildlife can live alongside one another.A new stage in Niger’s wildlife recoveryThe release gives the North African ostrich a new opportunity to occupy part of its former habitat in Niger. Kolmården says the species is currently found in Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, Senegal and Tunisia, while Niger lost its last wild bird in 2004.Niger has had a national strategy for conserving the North African ostrich since 2016. Kolmården says the strategy includes breeding birds with the eventual goal of releasing them into the wild. At the time described on its project website, 3 breeding centres held around 50 ostriches in the country.Sahara Conservation said the longer-term aim is to build a viable wild population in Gadabedji that can contribute to restoring the species across its historical range in Niger.

articles.title: Scientists first noticed Alaska rivers turning orange in 2018; new research finds waters in pristine areas can be more acidic and metal-rich than drainage from metal mines
articles.summary: The orange colour creeping through some of Alaska’s rivers is more than an unusual change in appearance; it is a sign that the chemistry of the water is
articles.body: The orange colour creeping through some of Alaska’s rivers is more than an unusual change in appearance; it is a sign that the chemistry of the water is changing too. The phenomenon first caught scientists’ attention in 2018, when once-clear streams in Alaska’s Brooks Range began showing striking orange and rust-coloured sections. Many of the affected waterways are in remote areas, far from the kind of industrial activity normally associated with polluted rivers. As permafrost thaws, water can move deeper into the ground and interact with minerals that were previously less exposed to flowing water, releasing acidity and metals. A new study published in AGU Advances has now examined six watersheds to understand what is happening to the water and how far the changes can spread.Orange water, but a much bigger change underneathThe rusty colour is produced when iron released through these mineral-weathering reactions oxidises, forming orange-coloured deposits. But iron is only part of the story. Water moving through the affected areas can pick up sulfate and a range of metals as it passes through mineral-rich rock. The process is known as acid rock drainage. It can happen naturally, without a mine or other industrial source being present. That distinction matters in Alaska. The orange streams are not simply abandoned mine sites being washed into rivers. Instead, the landscape itself contains minerals capable of producing acidic drainage when conditions change.Thawing permafrost may be helping to create those conditions. Frozen ground affects where water can travel underground. As it thaws, water can penetrate deeper into the landscape and come into contact with sulfide-bearing minerals. When water reaches these minerals, they can weather and release acidity and metals into the drainage. The result can be seen on the riverbanks as orange deposits, but the more important changes are taking place in the water itself.What scientists found in six watershedsResearchers examined six watersheds in Alaska’s Brooks Range between 2022 and 2024, collecting samples from rivers, tributaries and hillside seeps. The chemistry of some of the seeps was particularly striking. Their median pH was 3.2, compared with 8.3 in upstream mainstem rivers. The seeps also contained much higher concentrations of metals and sulfate. Across 23 measured metals, the median combined concentration in the acidic seeps was about 451 milligrams per litre. In the upstream mainstem waters, it was only about 0.1 milligrams per litre. Some of the drainage was chemically similar to water associated with acid mine drainage. In certain cases, concentrations of metals such as zinc, nickel and cadmium were comparable to or even higher than those reported from mine-affected waters in the region.The comparison is striking, but it does not mean the rivers are being polluted by abandoned mines. The study describes the process as natural acid rock drainage. The minerals are part of the underlying landscape, and changing conditions are allowing them to interact more strongly with water.The chemistry can travel downstreamThe orange colour may be most obvious close to the source, but the material released there does not necessarily stay in the same place. As acidic water enters larger rivers, it can be diluted and buffered. That helps explain why the main channels do not always become highly acidic even when they receive water from much more acidic tributaries and seeps.Metals and other substances can still move downstream, however. In the Salmon River, the researchers found elevated levels of sulfate, iron, zinc, nickel and cadmium as far as about 97 kilometres downstream from where the drainage entered the river. Some concentrations were as much as 70 times higher than those measured upstream. That makes the phenomenon more than a local curiosity. A small orange stream in a remote part of the Brooks Range can introduce material that eventually becomes detectable much farther along the river. The researchers point out that these waterways support fish and other aquatic life and are important to communities in the Arctic. Changes in water chemistry therefore raise questions about how continued drainage could affect river ecosystems, particularly in areas where the process is becoming more widespread.Why a warming Arctic may be changing the riversLong-term records offered another clue. In some of the watersheds, sulfate and zinc concentrations rose sharply between 2019 and 2020, with individual increases of up to 263% recorded in the available monitoring data. The timing followed unusually warm conditions and heavy snowfall in the region. The connection to permafrost is important because frozen ground controls how water moves through Arctic landscapes. When it thaws, pathways that were once blocked can open up. Water can then reach deeper rocks, allowing mineral reactions to occur more readily. There is also evidence that the process does not necessarily remain at the same intensity every year. In the Wulik and Agashashok watersheds, sulfate and zinc levels rose sharply before declining between 2021 and 2024. That suggests the chemistry of these drainage systems can change over time rather than simply becoming steadily more acidic.Scientists are now watching the rivers as a way of understanding what a changing Arctic landscape could mean for water quality. The orange colour is the most visible warning sign, but it is what the water carries that has drawn the researchers’ attention. What began as an unusual sight in a handful of remote Alaskan streams has turned into a much broader scientific question: as permafrost continues to thaw, how much more of the minerals locked beneath the surface could become exposed to moving water?

articles.title: In 2021, scientists threw 1,500 Christmas trees into a lake; three years later, they had completely transformed the ecosystem
articles.summary: What happens when thousands of Christmas trees are thrown into a lake?
articles.body: What happens when thousands of Christmas trees are thrown into a lake? In southeastern Finland, scientists set out to find the answer by deliberately submerging 1,500 spruce trees in Lake Saimaa as part of an unusual experiment designed to study their impact on aquatic life.The project began in 2021, when researchers from the Finnish Environment Institute (SYKE) placed groups of spruce trees on the bottom of the lake. The aim was to determine whether the trees could create an underwater habitat for organisms and fish, effectively turning parts of the lakebed into a kind of submerged forest.Three years later, researchers retrieved the trees and examined the areas where they had been placed. What they found was a dramatic increase in life around the submerged trees, particularly among organisms living on or near the lakebed.The trees were placed in groups of six to eight and submerged at a depth of about two metres. Bricks were used to keep them in position underwater. The experiment was designed to examine whether the natural structure of the trees could provide shelter and food for aquatic organisms.Benthic animals surgeKari-Matti Vuori, the scientist leading the research, said the experiment resulted in a major increase in benthic production in areas where the trees had been submerged. Benthic organisms are animals and other living organisms that live on, in or close to the bottom of aquatic ecosystems. They form an important part of the food chain, providing food for fish and other species.According to Vuori, the number of individual benthic animals increased tenfold in areas containing the submerged trees. Species diversity also increased dramatically, rising by as much as five times compared with the conditions recorded before the experiment. The difference was identified by comparing benthic samples collected from the lake before and after the trees were introduced.The submerged trees appeared to provide a new physical structure for organisms to colonise. Microbial and fungal communities developed around the wood, creating an additional source of food and helping establish a more complex underwater habitat.The effects were also noticed higher up the food chain. Local fishermen told Vuori that they had observed a considerable increase in the number of fish in areas where the trees had been placed. While the observations from fishermen were not the same as controlled scientific measurements, they added to the researchers' interest in how the submerged trees were influencing the ecosystem.Christmas trees as underwater habitatsThe experiment also highlighted how natural materials such as discarded Christmas trees can potentially be repurposed rather than simply thrown away. Once submerged, the trees provide branches and surfaces that can be used as shelter by aquatic organisms. As the wood gradually breaks down, it can also support microbial and fungal growth, creating food sources for smaller organisms that are themselves eaten by fish.The Finnish experiment was therefore not simply about disposing of old Christmas trees. It was designed to investigate whether the trees could contribute to aquatic biodiversity by creating additional habitat in the lake. The findings also connect to a broader environmental question: what happens to Christmas trees after the holiday season?Christmas trees are organic material and contain carbon that was absorbed while the trees were growing. Environmental experts have warned against sending them to landfill because decomposing organic waste can contribute to methane emissions. John Kazer, a footprint certification expert at the Carbon Trust, told the BBC that trees should be prevented from ending up in landfills where they can contribute to greenhouse gas emissions.However, the Finnish experiment does not mean Christmas trees should simply be dumped into lakes. The trees in the Lake Saimaa study were deliberately placed under controlled conditions as part of scientific research. Instead, the experiment offered an unusual glimpse into how a familiar seasonal object can become part of an aquatic ecosystem.Three years after 1,500 spruce trees were submerged in Lake Saimaa, researchers found that the underwater structures had become hotspots for benthic life, with the number of individual organisms increasing tenfold and species diversity rising as much as fivefold. What began as an experiment involving discarded Christmas trees had effectively demonstrated how submerged wood can provide new habitat and support aquatic food webs.
